paragraphs: Camera relocalization estimates where a camera is and how it is oriented from an image. This paper develops a scene-independent framework that uses 3D Gaussian Splatting both to establish an initial camera pose and to refine it. The same scene representation therefore supports two complementary parts of the localization process.

First, GS-RelocNet matches pixels in the input RGB image with Gaussians in the 3D scene. These 2D-to-3D correspondences provide an initial pose estimate. A second network improves that estimate using an image rendered from the Gaussian representation. The first stage incorporates unidirectional fusion between 2D and 3D features, while the refinement stage uses bidirectional fusion between image features to improve information sharing.

Experiments on 7 Scenes, Cambridge Landmarks, TUM RGB-D, and Bonn report state-of-the-art performance. The results also support the contribution of both fusion modules and pose refinement. These findings suggest that combining correspondence estimation with rendering-based refinement is a productive use of Gaussian scene representations; the authors present a universal localization pipeline as a direction for further research.
neurips-2025-3d-gaussian-splatting-based.tldr: A two-stage camera relocalization framework uses 3D Gaussians for image-to-scene matching and rendered-image pose refinement, achieving state-of-the-art benchmark results.

paragraphs: An artificial teammate must coordinate with partners whose preferences and behavior may be unfamiliar or change during an interaction. Time pressure makes this especially difficult: the agent needs to recognize a partner's strategy while choosing its own actions. This paper develops a cooperator that conditions its behavior on learned categories of partner strategies.

The framework first uses a variational autoencoder to compress agent trajectories into a latent strategy space. Clustering that space identifies distinct strategy types. The researchers then generate partners belonging to these types and train a cooperator to respond appropriately to each cluster. During interaction with a new partner, a fixed-share regret minimization algorithm continually updates the estimated partner strategy, allowing the cooperator to adjust its response.

Evaluation uses a modified Overcooked environment, where two players coordinate cooking tasks across a diverse strategy space, together with an online user study. The authors report state-of-the-art performance against existing baselines with unfamiliar human and artificial teammates. The findings support combining learned strategy categories with ongoing online adaptation in this collaborative setting.
neurips-2025-adaptively-coordinating-wit.tldr: A cooperator learns categories of partner strategies and updates its estimate during interaction to coordinate more effectively with unfamiliar teammates.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization chooses feasible decisions over successive rounds while controlling regret, the accumulated disadvantage relative to a fixed comparator. Standard projected methods can achieve optimal square-root-in-time regret, but projecting onto a complicated feasible set may be expensive. Separation-based alternatives avoid these projections, yet existing guarantees can deteriorate badly when the set is geometrically uneven.

The paper measures this unevenness through asphericity: the ratio of the smallest enclosing ball's radius to the largest inscribed ball's radius. Its algorithm reduces the problem to online optimization over dynamically updated ellipsoids. This construction draws on the classical ellipsoid method and accesses the original feasible set through a separation oracle.

The resulting regret bound is Õ(√(dT) + d²), with only logarithmic dependence on asphericity. Here d is dimension and T is the number of rounds. The method uses Õ(1) separation queries per round and avoids costly geometric preprocessing. Its contribution is a substantially milder dependence on difficult set geometry while retaining a small per-round oracle requirement.
neurips-2025-an-ellipsoid-algorithm-for-.tldr: Dynamically updated ellipsoids enable projection-free online convex optimization with regret that depends only logarithmically on feasible-set asphericity.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models often connect a pretrained vision encoder to a language model through a projector. Training this connection to produce captions does not fully explain how individual image tokens acquire meaning for the language model. This paper examines both the information compressed by the projector and the alignment between image patches and semantic words.

The analysis finds that the projector removes substantial redundant visual information while retaining elements needed for visual understanding. However, caption-based training improves patch-level semantic alignment only to a limited extent, leaving it weak and coarse. The authors propose a multi-semantic alignment hypothesis and introduce patch-aligned training to strengthen this finer-grained connection between visual regions and language.

Experiments show stronger compression, better patch alignment, and higher-quality captions. Under the same supervised fine-tuning setting, the paper reports improvements of 16% on referring expression grounding, 4% on question answering, and 3% on instruction-following benchmarks. These findings link better local visual-language alignment to improvements across several downstream tasks, beyond caption generation alone.
neurips-2025-analyzing-fine-grained-alig.tldr: Patch-aligned training strengthens the connection between image regions and semantic words, improving captions and several multimodal tasks.

paragraphs: Prediction-powered inference uses machine learning predictions on abundant unlabelled data to make statistical estimation more efficient when true labels are scarce. Existing procedures preserve confidence-interval validity at a fixed analysis time. This paper asks how to extend that benefit to settings where both labelled and unlabelled datasets continue growing.

The proposed answer is a prediction-powered confidence sequence: a sequence of uncertainty intervals designed for inference across time. The construction uses Ville's inequality and the method of mixtures. Its stated guarantee is asymptotic validity uniformly over time, an important qualification when interpreting the paper's anytime-valid framing. The target is a time-uniform guarantee rather than validity solely at one predetermined sample size.

The method also incorporates prior knowledge about prediction quality, allowing that information to further improve statistical efficiency. This connects the usefulness of machine predictions with what is already known about their reliability. The authors explain the design choices and demonstrate the procedures on real and synthetic examples, extending prediction-powered inference to continuing data collection.
neurips-2025-anytime-valid-bayes-assiste.tldr: Prediction-powered confidence sequences incorporate prior knowledge of prediction quality and provide asymptotic validity uniformly over time as data accumulate.

paragraphs: Recognizing closely related bird species requires visual expertise that can develop over many learning experiences. CleverBirds provides a benchmark for tracking that expertise in people. Its central task is to infer a learner's knowledge state from their history of multiple-choice answers, helping researchers study how fine-grained visual recognition develops over time.

The dataset comes from quizzes collected through the citizen-science platform eBird. More than 40,000 participants answered over 17 million questions covering more than 10,000 species. Participants answered about 400 questions on average, providing extended response histories rather than only isolated observations. The large number of species also creates a broad collection of concepts whose acquisition can be studied.

The paper finds that predicting learners' knowledge remains challenging, particularly across participant subgroups and question types. Contextual information provides different amounts of predictive benefit depending on its form. These results make the benchmark useful for evaluating whether knowledge-tracing methods capture differences among learners and questions, while supporting research into the development of visual expertise.
neurips-2025-cleverbirds-a-multiple-choi.tldr: CleverBirds provides millions of bird-identification quiz responses to study and predict how people's fine-grained visual expertise develops.

paragraphs: CogPhys studies whether remote sensors can estimate cognitive load, meaning the mental effort involved in activities such as reading, memorizing, and solving mathematics problems. It introduces an open-source dataset and associated hardware system that record multiple remote sensing modalities alongside contact-based physiological measurements, creating a shared basis for comparing these approaches.

The recordings combine RGB, near-infrared, thermal, and radio-frequency sensors with devices such as pulse oximeters and chest bands. Rather than connecting sensor recordings directly to cognitive labels alone, the benchmark uses intermediate physiological signals: pulse-related waveforms, respiration, and blinking. NASA-TLX survey responses establish personalized thresholds for high and low cognitive load, accounting for differences in reported effort between individuals.

Combining sensing modalities improves remote vital-sign estimation, with the fusion model achieving error below three beats per minute. For cognitive-load classification, remote pulse, respiratory, and blink signals achieve 86.49% accuracy, compared with 87.5% for contact-based sensing. The close benchmark results support the feasibility of cognitive monitoring with less intrusive remote measurements.
neurips-2025-cogphys-assessing-cognitive.tldr: CogPhys combines remote physiological sensors to classify cognitive load with benchmark accuracy approaching contact-based sensing.

paragraphs: Some species look so similar that appearance alone offers little help in distinguishing them. CrypticBio targets these visually confusing groups across a wide range of taxa. Its curation draws on observed misidentifications among iNaturalist community annotators, grounding the dataset in confusion that occurs during real biodiversity observation.

The dataset contains 52,000 cryptic groups spanning 67,000 species and 166 million images. Records combine research-grade image annotations with scientific and multilingual species terminology, hierarchical taxonomy, geographic and temporal context, and cryptic-group membership. This multimodal structure supplies complementary information for cases where visual distinctions are subtle. An open-source tool, CrypticBio-Curate, supports the construction of subsets for particular research needs.

The authors benchmark foundation models on subsets covering common, unseen, endangered, and invasive species. They find that spatial and temporal context has a substantial impact on zero-shot vision-language identification of cryptic species. The contribution is both a large resource for studying species ambiguity and evidence that contextual information matters for this difficult recognition problem.
neurips-2025-crypticbio-a-large-multimod.tldr: CrypticBio combines images, taxonomy, and contextual information at large scale to study identification of visually confusing species.

paragraphs: Event cameras produce asynchronous streams, which fit poorly into neural architectures designed around conventional image frames. DERD-Net estimates depth from these streams in both monocular and stereo setups. It uses the geometric structure of event observations to create a representation that a neural network can process locally.

Given known camera poses, the method back-projects events into space and records ray densities in disparity space images. A network combines 3D convolutions with recurrence to recognize depth-related patterns in local subregions. This local design supports parallel inference and, according to the paper, keeps model complexity and memory costs constant and very low regardless of camera resolution.

On MVSEC and DSEC, monocular results are comparable to existing stereo methods. With stereo input, the authors report at least a 42% reduction in mean absolute error relative to state-of-the-art approaches. They also report more than threefold greater depth completeness while reducing median absolute error by at least 30%. These findings support event-ray densities as an effective representation for depth learning under the stated camera-pose requirement.
neurips-2025-derd-net-learning-depth-fro.tldr: DERD-Net learns depth from local event-ray densities using known camera poses, reporting substantial stereo accuracy and depth-completeness gains.

paragraphs: Methods that reconstruct 3D scenes by predicting pointmaps can work well when the scene is static. Moving objects complicate this process because changes between views cannot be explained solely by the camera's motion. This paper addresses the resulting reconstruction problems in methods such as DUSt3R, whose original design targets static scenes.

The proposed D²USt3R directly predicts Static-Dynamic Aligned Pointmaps. These pointmaps represent both stationary and moving scene geometry while explicitly incorporating spatial and temporal information. The key change is therefore in what the model predicts: an aligned representation that accounts for scene dynamics. The authors describe this representation as capturing dense 3D correspondences, which can also support downstream tasks.

Across datasets containing complex motions, the experiments report consistently better 3D reconstruction performance. These results support explicitly representing dynamic geometry when reconstructing scenes with moving objects. The contribution is a way to extend pointmap-based reconstruction to the spatial and temporal relationships that camera-pose alignment alone cannot capture in dynamic settings.
neurips-2025-enhancing-3d-reconstruction.tldr: D²USt3R predicts pointmaps that align static and moving geometry, improving reconstruction across datasets with complex scene motion.

paragraphs: Activating connections in a network consumes resources, but minimizing that cost can conflict with providing sufficient access to different groups. Fair Minimum Labeling formalizes the task of scheduling edge activations so that each node group meets specified coverage requirements for reaching a target set, while keeping total activation cost as low as possible.

The formulation applies to temporal networks supporting activities such as distributed data collection, update dissemination, and service restoration. The authors prove that the optimization problem is NP-hard and has an approximation hardness bound of order log |V|, where |V| is the number of nodes. They also develop probabilistic approximation algorithms that match this bound, establishing the best possible stated approximation guarantee for activation cost.

A practical evaluation studies fair aggregation of data from multiple sources to train a shared model. The method satisfies group-level fairness requirements at substantially lower activation cost than baseline heuristics. The results connect the theoretical formulation to a concrete learning task where equitable network access and resource efficiency must be addressed together.
neurips-2025-fair-minimum-labeling-effic.tldr: Fair Minimum Labeling schedules network connections to meet group coverage requirements at low cost, with approximation guarantees matching the stated hardness bound.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains across clients whose datasets may differ substantially in their labels and features. These differences can pull local training toward inconsistent objectives and reduce global model performance. Flick addresses this heterogeneity by generating synthetic data informed by both client-specific information and knowledge from an existing large language model.

Each client summarizes its local data in text. The central server combines insights across these summaries to guide the language model toward task-relevant knowledge and produce informative prompts. A generative model then uses those prompts to create synthetic examples. The examples support both global model fine-tuning and compensation for local data gaps, gradually bringing client label and feature distributions into closer alignment.

Experiments on three datasets report global accuracy improvements of up to 11.43% and convergence acceleration of up to 12.9 times. These are reported maximum gains across the evaluations. The findings support using language-guided data generation to address differences among client datasets, with synthetic examples serving as the mechanism for improving alignment.
neurips-2025-flick-empowering-federated-.tldr: Flick uses client summaries and language-model knowledge to generate synthetic data that improves federated learning under heterogeneous client distributions.

paragraphs: A long reasoning attempt can contain a pivotal step where the model's next choice strongly affects whether it succeeds. Optimization methods that treat the entire attempt as a single unit may miss this structure. Guided Pivotal Optimization, or GPO, focuses training on these critical points within a generated reasoning trajectory.

GPO estimates an advantage function to locate a critical step. It then returns the generation process to that point, samples new continuations, and prioritizes learning from those rollouts. This gives the optimization procedure additional experience with consequential reasoning decisions. The approach is designed as a general fine-tuning strategy that can be combined with different optimization methods.

The paper provides theoretical analysis and experiments on challenging reasoning benchmarks. In those experiments, adding GPO consistently and significantly improves the tested optimization methods. The findings support the idea that where training examples branch within a reasoning process matters: concentrating new continuations around pivotal moments can make the surrounding optimization procedure more effective.
neurips-2025-gpo-learning-from-critical-.tldr: GPO improves reasoning training by identifying critical steps, sampling new continuations from them, and prioritizing those rollouts.

paragraphs: Graph models may need to learn from a succession of different graph domains while retaining what they learned earlier. GraphKeeper addresses this domain-incremental setting, where new training can cause catastrophic forgetting. It targets two sources of instability: changes in learned graph embeddings and deviations in the model's decision boundary.

To reduce embedding shifts and confusion between domains, GraphKeeper combines domain-specific parameter-efficient fine-tuning with objectives that disentangle knowledge within and across domains. A knowledge-preservation component aims to maintain a stable decision boundary as additional domains arrive. When a graph's domain is unobserved, a domain-aware distribution discrimination mechanism helps obtain an appropriate embedding.

The experiments report state-of-the-art results, with improvements of 6.5% to 16.6% over the runner-up and negligible forgetting. The authors also demonstrate integration with several representative graph foundation models. These findings support treating representation stability and decision-boundary stability together when extending graph models across domains, with applicability demonstrated across multiple underlying model choices.
neurips-2025-graphkeeper-graph-domain-in.tldr: GraphKeeper combines domain-specific adaptation and knowledge preservation to learn across graph domains with negligible forgetting in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Multiple visual experts can give vision-language models complementary strengths, but using several experts increases training and inference costs. HAWAII transfers knowledge from multiple teachers into a single vision encoder. The goal is to retain useful expertise from several sources with minimal additional computation in the resulting model.

The framework uses teacher-specific low-rank adaptation adapters and a router to handle different teachers' knowledge. Aligning each adapter with one teacher is intended to reduce conflicting or noisy supervision. Knowledge transfer then operates at two levels: fine-grained distillation emphasizes informative visual tokens using adaptive importance scores, while coarse-grained distillation summarizes knowledge across teachers into routed general-knowledge adapters.

Experiments across vision-language tasks report better performance than popular open-source vision-language models. The findings support a hierarchical approach to distillation in which teacher-specific details and broader shared knowledge receive different treatment. This organization matters because successful compression into one encoder must manage differences among teachers as well as preserve the complementary information they provide.
neurips-2025-hawaii-hierarchical-visual-.tldr: HAWAII distills multiple visual experts into one encoder using routed adapters and fine- and coarse-grained knowledge transfer.

paragraphs: When multiple agents learn strategies independently, their updates can become misaligned. Optimistic Follow-the-Regularized-Leader addresses this by incorporating predictions of future rewards, but delayed observations make those predictions harder to use effectively. This paper proves that even a one-step feedback delay can worsen the method's social regret and convergence behavior.

The proposed Weighted OFTRL increases the weight placed on the next-reward prediction vector. The central idea is that stronger optimism can compensate for delayed information. The theoretical condition is explicit: the optimistic weight must exceed the feedback delay for the paper's stated recovery guarantees to hold.

Under that condition, the authors prove constant social regret in general-sum normal-form games. They separately prove that the actual strategy iterates converge to a Nash equilibrium in polymatrix zero-sum games. These guarantees concern different game classes and different aspects of learning behavior. Experiments support and strengthen the theoretical results, showing the value of adjusting prediction weight when learning from delayed feedback.
neurips-2025-learning-from-delayed-feedb.tldr: Weighting reward predictions more heavily than the feedback delay restores stated regret and convergence guarantees for optimistic learning in specified game classes.

paragraphs: Smaller evaluation suites can save computation and make results easier to interpret, but choosing a representative subset of metrics requires defining what representation means. Metritocracy uses social choice theory to formalize this question. It examines how metric selection preserves the positions of the alternatives being evaluated, such as language models or hospitals.

The first proposed property, positional representation, requires every alternative to receive sufficient representation at every ranking-position cutoff. The second, positional proportionality, controls how far an alternative can be proportionally overrepresented or underrepresented at any position. These definitions turn an informal preference for a balanced subset into explicit properties that can be analyzed.

The authors prove upper and lower bounds on the smallest metric subset needed to guarantee each property in the worst case. They also generalize the properties to incorporate specified groups of metrics that must be represented. Case studies in language-model and hospital-quality evaluation connect the theory to practical selection problems, clarifying what a reduced benchmark can be required to preserve.
neurips-2025-metritocracy-representative.tldr: Metritocracy defines formal representation guarantees for reduced metric suites and bounds how many metrics are needed to achieve them.

paragraphs: This paper studies how unregularized gradient descent generalizes in separable linear classification with multiple classes. It establishes population-risk bounds for losses that decay toward zero. The central finding is that convergence depends crucially on the geometry of the loss template, the structure used to define the multiclass loss, rather than simply the geometry of the resulting loss function.

The analysis provides risk upper bounds for arbitrary loss decay rates when the template is smooth with respect to a p-norm. For exponentially decaying losses, the number of classes enters the guarantees very differently depending on that geometry. The p = ∞ case has logarithmic dependence on the class count, whereas the p = 2 case scales linearly.

A lower bound for the latter setting establishes that polynomial dependence on the class count is unavoidable there. The proof develops a Rademacher-complexity bound for low-noise, vector-valued linear predictors under general p-norm template smoothness. Together, these results show why multiclass loss-template geometry can materially affect generalization guarantees as the number of classes grows.
neurips-2025-multiclass-loss-geometry-ma.tldr: For separable multiclass linear classification, loss-template geometry determines sharply different class-count dependence in gradient descent's generalization bounds.

paragraphs: PHYBench evaluates language-model reasoning through 500 original physics problems, ranging from high-school material to Physics Olympiad difficulty. The benchmark targets problems in existing evaluations: overly simple tasks, contaminated data, and flawed questions. Original content addresses contamination concerns, while systematic curation is used to remove defective items.

The problems elicit reasoning across multiple steps and conditions. Evaluations report greater token use and stronger differentiation among reasoning models than AIME 2024, OlympiadBench, and GPQA. The strongest evaluated model, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reaches 36.9% accuracy, compared with 61.9% for human experts. This gap indicates substantial remaining difficulty on the benchmark's curated physics tasks.

The paper also introduces an Expression Edit Distance score for assessing mathematical expressions. It reports a 204% improvement in sample efficiency over binary scoring, providing a more informative evaluation signal than a simple correct-or-incorrect outcome. Together, the problem set and scoring method support examination of reasoning robustness, preferences, and deficiencies in demanding physical reasoning.
neurips-2025-phybench-holistic-evaluatio.tldr: PHYBench uses 500 original physics problems and expression-based scoring to distinguish reasoning models and expose a substantial gap from human experts.

paragraphs: Vision transformers can repurpose image-patch tokens to store information about the whole image. In DINOv2, this produces attention-map artifacts that harm interpretability and dense image tasks. Adding register tokens gives the model dedicated places to store global information, producing cleaner attention maps. This paper investigates what those cleaner maps actually reveal.

The authors find that, in large models, cleaned-up attention maps do not accurately reflect how local image information contributes to global features. Instead, global information is dominated by information extracted from register tokens, creating a disconnect between local and global representations. The visual appearance of an attention map therefore does not by itself establish that it faithfully explains local information integration.

The analysis also identifies a similar phenomenon caused by the classification, or [CLS], token in models without explicit registers. This broadens the finding beyond register-equipped architectures. By attributing the behavior to these specific tokens, the work identifies an architectural source of interpretability problems and suggests a direction for developing more interpretable vision models.
neurips-2025-register-and-cls-tokens-ind.tldr: Register and [CLS] tokens can disconnect local and global features in large vision transformers, making clean attention maps misleading as explanations.

paragraphs: scPilot connects a language model's reasoning process directly to single-cell RNA sequencing data and bioinformatics tools. The model interacts in natural language while inspecting the data needed for its analysis. The framework turns cell-type annotation, developmental-trajectory reconstruction, and transcription-factor targeting into problems that require step-by-step decisions and supporting evidence.

A central feature is revision: the model can obtain new evidence and reconsider its earlier conclusions. The authors call this omics-native reasoning because the analysis is grounded in the underlying molecular data and tools. They also release scBench, comprising nine expertly curated datasets and graders for evaluating this capability across language models.

Compared with one-shot prompting, iterative reasoning with o1 improves average cell-type annotation accuracy by 11%, while Gemini 2.5 Pro reduces trajectory graph-edit distance by 30%. These results concern different models and tasks. The generated reasoning traces explain issues such as ambiguous marker genes and regulatory logic, making the analysis process available for inspection alongside its predictions.
neurips-2025-scpilot-large-language-mode.tldr: scPilot grounds iterative language-model reasoning in single-cell data and tools, improving reported analysis results while producing auditable reasoning traces.

paragraphs: Segmentation masks specify where objects should appear, while regional text prompts describe what those objects should be. Seg2Any combines these inputs to address a persistent image-generation challenge: matching object shapes and semantic attributes simultaneously. The framework builds on multimodal diffusion transformers and separates the two kinds of guidance.

Regional semantics enter through an attention mask that connects entities to their assigned prompts. Shape information enters through an Entity Contour Map, which represents boundaries and is processed as an additional modality. A separate attribute-isolation mechanism restricts each entity's image tokens to attending within that entity during image self-attention, aiming to prevent attributes from leaking between objects.

The authors also introduce SACap-1M, with one million images, 5.9 million segmented entities, and detailed regional captions, plus the SACap-Eval benchmark. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on both open-set and closed-set mask-to-image benchmarks, especially for fine spatial and attribute control. These findings support treating boundaries, regional meaning, and inter-entity attribute separation as distinct components of controllable image generation.
neurips-2025-seg2any-open-set-segmentati.tldr: Seg2Any separates regional semantics, object contours, and attribute isolation to improve shape and semantic control in mask-guided image generation.

paragraphs: Sparse support recovery identifies which entries of a mostly zero signal are nonzero using noisy measurements. This paper studies measurements that themselves involve only a limited number of signal entries. It establishes sufficient sample-size conditions and compares them with known necessary conditions to quantify the measurement cost of sparse designs.

Let p be signal dimension, s the number of nonzero signal entries, and d the expected number of nonzeros per measurement row. In the regime ds/p → ∞, the combined results give a phase transition at Θ(s log(p/s) / log(ds/p)) measurements. The stated inflation factor, log(s) / log(ds/p), expresses how restricting each measurement's coverage increases the number of measurements required.

The paper separately examines sparsifying an originally dense measurement matrix. When s = αp and d = ψp, with α and ψ between zero and one and ψ small, it gives a sufficient sample size of Θ(p/ψ²). This second result is conditional on a uniform integrability conjecture whose proof remains in progress; it is therefore a qualified sufficiency statement.
neurips-2025-the-price-of-sparsity-suffi.tldr: The paper quantifies sparse-measurement sample complexity and gives a separate, conjecture-dependent sufficient bound for sparsifying dense measurements.

paragraphs: Human motion prediction must produce diverse, physically plausible future poses from a short observed history. WaveAR addresses limitations associated with converting motion into vector-quantized tokens, which can restrict fidelity and training stability. Its approach performs autoregressive generation in a continuous latent representation while incorporating motion information at multiple frequency scales.

A lightweight spatiotemporal variational autoencoder first compresses sequences of 3D joints into a shorter latent stream. Masked autoregressive prediction then operates directly on these continuous latents, using available latents and spectral cues from a two-dimensional discrete wavelet transform. Alternating cross-attention and self-attention layers combine temporal context with low- and high-frequency wavelet components. A small diffusion head predicts noise residuals for individual tokens.

The continuous representation avoids vector quantization, while localized frequency information helps preserve fine motion details. Experiments on standard benchmarks report more accurate and computationally efficient predictions than prior state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining compact continuous motion representations with multiscale spectral guidance for efficient, detailed future-motion generation.
neurips-2025-wavear-wavelet-aware-contin.tldr: WaveAR combines continuous autoregressive diffusion with wavelet guidance to improve human-motion prediction accuracy and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Reconstructing visual experiences from fMRI often relies on a model trained or fine-tuned for each individual. ZEBRA addresses the challenge of applying a decoder to an unseen person without subject-specific adaptation. Its central idea is to separate information about the person from information about the visual content represented in their brain activity.

The framework decomposes fMRI representations into subject-related and semantic-related components. Adversarial training explicitly encourages this separation so that the semantic representation remains informative about visual content while being invariant to subject identity. This is the mechanism intended to enable transfer across people without collecting additional fMRI data for adaptation or retraining the model for the new subject.

Experiments show significant improvements over zero-shot baselines and performance comparable to fully fine-tuned models on several metrics. The comparison is qualified by those metrics rather than establishing equivalence across all measures. These findings support separating subject identity from visual semantics as a practical route toward brain-image decoding that scales beyond individually adapted models.
neurips-2025-zebra-towards-zero-shot-cro.tldr: ZEBRA disentangles subject identity from visual semantics to reconstruct images from unseen subjects' fMRI without subject-specific adaptation.
